questions.question: What is the difference between Git and GitHub?
options: They are exactly the same thing with different names
Git is the underlying version control tool that works locally; GitHub is a hosted service built around Git adding collaboration features like pull requests and code review
GitHub is a programming language, Git is a code editor
Git only works for Python, GitHub only for JavaScript
questions.explanation: Git tracks changes to code and works entirely on a local machine. GitHub (or similar services like GitLab) hosts Git repositories and adds collaboration tooling like pull requests, review, and CI/CD integration.

questions.question: What causes a merge conflict?
options: Two branches change the exact same lines of a file differently, and Git cannot automatically decide which change is correct
A commit message is too long
A branch has too many commits
The internet connection was too slow during a push
questions.explanation: A merge conflict specifically occurs when overlapping changes exist on the same lines across two branches being merged, requiring a human to manually resolve which version (or combination) is correct.

questions.question: A release gets delayed by a merge conflict. Which question best helps a TPM assess whether this indicates a real process problem?
options: Can we just delete one engineer's branch to avoid the conflict?
Is this a one-off, quick-to-resolve conflict, or a sign of a deeper coordination problem with multiple teams constantly colliding on the same files?
Why does Git allow conflicts to happen at all?
Can we stop using version control to avoid this in the future?
questions.explanation: A single merge conflict is usually a normal, quick, mechanical fix. Frequent conflicts, however, can signal poor branch hygiene or insufficient coordination between engineers working on overlapping code — worth distinguishing before assuming either extreme.
